#4691. The Part of Your Holiday Hangover You Can’t See

FOUR GLASSES OF wine? Your liver drinks them, too. Extra gravy? Your liver probably would have liked for you to stop at the third scoop, but you’re in this together. Nearly every bite you eat and every drink you down ends up getting managed by the same organ in your body: your liver.

The liver is a workhorse that plays a role in over 500 bodily functions, which include filtering toxins, regulating blood sugar, processing cholesterol, and more. But come the holidays, all the food and festive drinking can put your body’s largest organ to the test. Here’s how the wreckage happens and how to avoid accumulating long-term damage.

WHEN YOU HAVE a drink or two, your liver kicks into gear and performs triage: It transforms alcohol into harmless water and carbon dioxide, which you then pee out or exhale. The liver also holds on to anything it can use, such as the antioxidants in wine or the carbs in beer. But that doesn’t mean alcohol is nutritious. Metabolizing alcohol also creates fatty acids along the way, which get stored as triglycerides—a kind of cholesterol—until your body can use them up. Typically, if you eat and drink moderately, your body processes them just fine. Until you...

THE MORE YOU drink, the more your liver shuffles those triglycerides into the “burn later” pile...until the pile is so big that your liver can’t get to the bottom of it.

“If you binge, then binge again, then binge again, your liver gets shocked each time and can’t recover,” says Christopher Koh, MD, clinical director at the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.

You may not feel the damage on your liver after the holiday or the next one. But over time, the holidays may overwhelm the organ. This can look like increased inflammation that eventually kills off liver cells, leaving scar tissue in their place (and can lead to cirrhosis, a problem in which 25- to 34-year-olds have the highest risk of death compared with other age groups). Not good. Experts say just three get-togethers a week through the holiday season can initiate inflammation if each outing involves more than five servings of alcohol in two hours. Not to mention when...

YOU DON’T EVEN have to drink alcohol to mess up your liver. Seasonal foods (you know the sides that are delicious but are high in saturated fat or refined carbs, along with processed red meat) combined with holiday-associated weight gain may increase the risk of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.

“It’s estimated that up to 30 percent of the US population has [MASLD], and there aren’t symptoms, so people usually don’t know and aren’t doing anything to reverse it,” says Mazen Noureddin, MD, hepatologist at Houston Methodist.

As obesity continues to rise, researchers estimate MASLD rates will rise to over 41 percent of the US population in 2050. That fat is wreaking the same havoc alcohol does—causing inflammation and eventual scarring—without the libations. MASLD may develop in as little as six weeks if you really overdo it.

YOU DON’T NEED to buy an activated-charcoal smoothie or a beet-juice detox cleanse to do it. Your liver can regenerate and naturally get itself back in working order if you move the heck out of its way. A month or so without a drop of alcohol (no beer during the game, no wine during date night) can reduce the fat storage in the liver and help tame inflammation. You can also undo some of the fat that causes MASLD by cleaning up your diet and cutting portion sizes: Losing 5 percent of your weight can reduce up to 25 percent of liver fat.

#4690. How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

#4689. Lifting Heavy Isn’t the Whole Story When It Comes to Building Strength. Here's What to Do Instead.

My name is Cori Ritchey, and I am an exercise physiology nerd turned fitness journalist, and the fitness editor at Women’s Health. When I’m not writing, editing, and researching fitness, I’m teaching it to my personal training and group fitness clients. In my new column, Between Sets, I’m pulling back the curtain on the same advice, tips, and ‘aha!’ moments I share with my clients while they’re catching their breath. Stick around for the strategic, science-backed nuggets that’ll help you move better, train smarter, and actually enjoy the process.

Scroll any fitness feed and you’ll see it: people clanging plates, chasing PRs, and even pulling dangerous stunts for the pride of lifting heavy. And where there’s real joy in getting stronger, there’s also real pressure to keep adding weight.

As a strength and conditioning coach and the fitness editor at Women’s Health, I’ve been preaching the lift-heavy-or-go-home gospel for years. For valid reason: challenging your muscles over time is one of the most reliable ways to build lasting strength, support bone health, improve body composition, and stay functional as we age.

The “lift heavy” ethos isn’t new. Strength training is as old as Ancient Greece, where the first gyms were developed. It progressed through decades of physical culture into Muscle Beach, USA, the birthplace of American lifting that started as a beachside gymnastics park in Venice Beach, California, in the 1940s. It was there, too, where the first American women bodybuilders, like legendary Abbey Stockton, emerged—at a time when many scientists still believed lifting was bad for the body.

Research eventually caught up to what lifters were already experiencing: resistance training works. More women, especially in recent years, started showing up for it, too. In 2004, 17 percent of women reported regularly participating in weight lifting. By 2020, that number has bumped to nearly 30 percent. Then came the influencer era, amplifying a message that’s equal parts motivating and misleading: lifting weights is good for you—but it has to be heavy to count.

There’s a kernel of truth in there. Progressive overload (the process of gradually increasing the stress you put on your body in a workout) builds muscle and strength, and increasing load is an efficient way to do so.

And that matters—especially when heavier, heavier, heavier simply isn’t in the cards.

Because for many, it’s not. It requires access to specific equipment, time to train consistently without rushing through sets, and quality coaching and information to nail form and stay injury-free. It also has to be safe and appropriate for your body on any given day—whether you’re navigating chronic illness, postpartum or perimenopause realities, and injury history, or limiting pain. And even when everything lines up on paper, there’s a very real mental hurdle: walking into a gym and loading up a bar can be intimidating as hell.

Still, if you’re here to build strength, change your body composition, protect your bone health, or invest in your movement longevity, lifting heavier will certainly help—but it’s not the only path to lifelong strength. Somewhere along the way, “heavy” became synonymous with “effective”, and “light” or "moderate" became codes for “waste of time.”

The exercise research world is finding that’s not the case. “You don't need to do anything heavy for the health benefits of resistance exercise to take place,” says Stuart Phillips, PhD, kinesiology professor and hypertrophy researcher at McMaster University.

Adequate research has suggested that hypertrophy (the fancy scientific term for muscle growth) is not determined by a magic rep goal or the weight on the bar, says Susie Reiner, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, assistant professor of exercise science at Seton Hall University, and CEO of TheoryEx, a sport science research and consulting firm. “Instead, hypertrophy appears to be driven by whether a training set provides a sufficiently strong internal stimulus to the muscle, which is reasonably defined as effort and proximity to muscular failure.”

Trainers have traditionally been taught that specific rep ranges map neatly to specific goals: 1 to 3 for power, 3 to 8 for strength, 8 to 12 for muscle, and 12-plus for muscular endurance. But newer findings show you can build muscle across a much wider rep range—roughly as low as 5 and as high as 25, Phillips says. “There is, then, by definition, no sweet spot for muscle building, because the whole repetition range then becomes the sweet spot.”

Across several studies and meta-analyses, similar muscle growth has been seen between people who train with lighter loads (about 30 to 40 percent of their one-rep maximum), and those who train with heavier loads (about 70 to 85 percent of their one-rep maximum)—as long as sets are taken close enough to failure.

Muscle growth is dependent on recruiting and fatiguing a large portion of muscle fibers, Reiner says. Your muscles need a reason to adapt. With heavier weights for fewer reps, you recruit a lot of fibers immediately. With lighter weights for higher reps, you recruit them more gradually.

One thing to note here: while a large percentage of these studies have only been done in men, Phillips notes that “the work that has been done in women shows us that actually men and women respond very, very similarly to weight lifting in terms of muscle mass gain. Women have less baseline muscle, but relatively speaking, they gain the same amount as men—that's been robustly shown.” Phillips and his colleagues are currently running several studies (including one study specific to perimenopausal women!) that will further clarify what this looks like in women.

Researchers feel confident that as long as sets are taken sufficiently to failure (more on what that means coming up), different loading strategies can produce similar hypertrophy, Reiner says.

Here’s what that looks like IRL: Let’s say you have biceps curls on your workout plan each week. One week, you pick up the 10-pound dumbbells, and do 3 sets of 12 reps. In the sets, when you approach the end of that rep range, it feels tough—you can maybe grind out 2 more reps max. The next week, you reach for the 15s. You can only hit 6 reps before you feel like your form is faltering, but the effort feels similar—you’ve still got about two reps left before your form breaks down.

The heavier weight might feel more empowering, but both workouts deliver a similar muscle-building stimulus—assuming you’re training regularly enough, eating enough protein and calories, and adequately recovering, of course.

Sure, research confirms you don’t have to lift crazy heavy—but that doesn’t mean that coming close to failure feels easy. Failing a rep can be scary (and honestly, discouraging). Here’s the good news: you don’t need true, all-out failure. You just need to train to proximity to failure.

One practical way to gauge that is with the rate of perceived exertion scale. “Rate of perceived exertion (RPE) is a global effort scale, typically ranging from one to 10,” Reiner says. An RPE of 10 represents maximal effort—no chance you could do one more rep. A RPE of nine suggests you could do one more, an RPE of eight means you could probably do two more reps, and so on and so forth.

Muscle growth still occurs between RPE of 7 to 9, Phillips says. “You don’t need it to be a 10 out of 10 where you’re red-lining and can’t get the bar off your chest.” In other words: you can train hard without routinely hitting the point where things get sketchy.

That matters, because the closer you get to all-out failure, the more your injury risk can creep up—especially if you start twisting, bouncing, and compensating to force a rep you simply don’t have.

The failure you want to flirt with is technical failure, or technical fatigue. “Technical failure means you cannot complete another repetition with good form,” Phillips says—that’s where injury risk rises. Muscular failure (otherwise known as momentary failure) occurs when a muscle is unable to generate enough force to complete another rep, regardless of maximal effort. Picture trying to do one more biceps curl and you quite literally cannot lift your arm and the weight up again—that’s muscular failure..

Aim for technical failure. Pushing yourself too far in an effort to achieve muscular failure could cause your body to overcompensate and push you into a compromising position. The good news, too, is technical failure tends to be very close to muscular failure for most people, Phillips says.

A useful rule of thumb: stop when you have one to two perfect-form reps left in the tank.

Yes, you still need to reach for that RPE of 7 to 9—but there’s more ways to do that than just reaching for the next highest weight. Here are some other elements you can play with to up the challenge:

Frequency. Reaching for heavier weights, you can simply aim to reach for any type of weight more often. That might look like increasing your strength training days from two to three days a week.

Volume. Think of your training volume as the amount of weight total you lift during a given session. Sure, lifting heavier loads is one way to increase your total, but it can also be accomplished by increasing the amount of sets or reps you do.

Rest time. Decreasing the amount of rest you allow yourself gives your muscles less time to recover, wearing them out quicker with lighter loads.

Time under tension. The amount of time your muscles work for matters. Increasing your time under tension, or the amount of time your muscles are working in a lift (for example, lowering a curl for a slow four-count).

That all being said, heavier loads might still take the cake in terms of efficiency. You’ll find yourself increasing your frequency and volume to monotonous levels if you never increase your load.

Back to biceps curls: Say you get comfortable at six reps at 15 lbs. After a few weeks, it no longer starts to feel challenging for you, so you increase it eight. And then 10. And then 12. If you never reach for the intimidating 20 lb dumbbells, you’ll eventually find yourself having to do sets of 30 reps just to feel something. And that can become time consuming. You don’t need extremes all the time—but you do need your training to stay challenging.

“For individuals who are uncomfortable training to very high levels of effort, consistent training at moderate-to-high RPEs combined with sufficient volume and progression can still produce meaningful muscle growth,” Reiner says. “From a long-term perspective, hypertrophy depends less on any single maximal set and more on repeated exposure to challenging, well-managed training over weeks and months.”

Convinced to start pushing closer to failure? Here are a few ways to progress safely.

The two-for-two method is a classic progression strategy used by professional trainers. Once you can do two extra proper-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load.

Let's use the biceps curl example just one more time. You’ve been training with the 15s for sets of 8, and now you can hit 10 with clean form for two workouts in a row. That’s your cue to grab 17.5s the next go.

How much should you increase, exactly? The National Strength and Conditioning Association’s guideline is 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. Reminder that this is just a general guide—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

Trying heavier weights is way less intimidating when you have a safety net.

If you’re nervous, ask for a spot. Maybe you already have a gym buddy you workout with regularly that can help pull the barbell up if you get stuck on a bench press. If you don’t, ask one of your gym’s trainers or employees. Most people will politely oblige, and will even appreciate your effort in challenging yourself.

Have a conversation with your spotter before you get into the lift. Tell them how many reps you’re aiming for, and a cue you’ll give them when you want them to jump in and help (my go-to is a simple “now”—since that’s about all you can get out when you’re out of breath).

Some days just don’t feel as strong as others. Maybe you didn’t sleep super well last night, stressed about work, or are at a tough point in your cycle. That’s life. When that happens, you need to respect the cues your body gives you.

If your warmup sets feel unusually heavy, take the hint: this just might not be the day to pick up that heavy weight. It doesn’t mean you’ve regressing, it’s just a bump in the road. Strength, and muscle building, is not a linear process.

Build muscle with the WH+ Build & Burn series

Ultimately, building and maintaining muscle mass is one of the strongest investments you can make in long-term health—especially as you age.

And lifting heavy is one effective way to provide muscle-building stimulus to the body—but it isn’t accessible, comfortable, or safe for everyone all the time. The goal is progressive challenge, and lighter loads can deliver that when you train with intention and effort.

“You do not need to lift heavy to build muscle, but you do need to train with intention,” Reiner says. “The best approach is the one that someone can perform consistently, safely, and with enough effort to challenge the muscle over time.”

Cori Ritchey, C.S.C.S., is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and condition coach and group fitness instructor. She’s reported on topics regarding health, nutrition, mental health, fitness, sex, and relationships for several years. You can find more of her work in Men’s Health, HealthCentral, Livestrong, Self, and others.

Prolactin and oxytocin are also associated with relaxation and sleep onset, which may help you fall asleep more easily and get deeper rest. Not sure exactly what to fill your fridge with? Start with leafy greens. Spinach helps dilate blood vessels, which can increase blood flow to the genitals. Other greens like kale, cabbage, and bok choy are good sources of folate, which helps reproductive health.

Next, make sure you're eating eggs. They're rich in B vitamins, which ease stress and support a healthy libido, leading to better orgasms.

As for what to avoid in your diet, Dr. Elist suggests limiting processed foods, added sugar, alcohol, sodium, and caffeine.

That said, if you’re prone to anxiety, keep it simple (i.e. close your eyes, dim the lights, wear earplugs) and short. The goal is heightened sensation, and you don’t want to feel trapped in your own head.

The frenulum is the small band of tissue on the underside of the penis connecting the head to the shaft, and since there are a ton of nerve endings in such a small area, it can be intensely sensitive for many men. If you or your partner stimulate it with a lighter touch, lips, tongue, or gentle vibration, it can create a different type of arousal than the standard base-to-head stroke. You may need more time and patience here, but the payoff can be a deeper, more memorable finish.

Notice how pretty much all of these tips involve trying something new or doing something you're used to, but in a new way? Yeah, there's a scientific reason for that. As we get “used to” certain sexual stimuli, we don’t get aroused in the same way—but new experiences can increase sexual desire and satisfaction, according to a research review in The Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy. Not only that, but a 2015 study in Evolutionary Psychological Science found a link between the novelty of experiences and the quality of orgasms in men.

Basically, if sex feels the same every time, your body adapts and your orgasms start to fall flat. Prezant compares it to hitting a gym plateau: same pressure, same position, same environment equals diminishing returns. Switching up the variables, even slightly—whether that’s time of day, pace, type of stimulation, or something else—can make a big difference in orgasm intensity.

#4686. The Secrets to Whole-Life Training

A well-rounded fitness routine that will enhance all of your activities and adventures starts with your feet.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There’s more to getting fit than chasing a PR or sweating through another bootcamp class. The real payoff? Being ready for the next workout, the weekend adventure, the everyday hustle, and all the years ahead.

The key is making different types of exercise work together, rather than relying on any one activity. This multifaceted and well-rounded approach to training means you’re working more than the muscles, because you’re focused on the movements.

When you approach training this way, you’re literally starting from the ground up. “Every single step you take, your foot is the first thing that hits the ground,” says Jen Perez, DC, a chiropractic physician who combines clinical practice and education to help people improve foot health and lower-body function. “It’s the first thing that interfaces with the world around you, what has to be strong and springy when you want to run or jump or dance or ski.”

A whole-life, well-rounded training plan comes down to five essentials, according to Courtney Conley, DC, a best-selling author and chiropractic physician with more than two decades of clinical experience:

Cardio and strength may already be part of your routine, but the others can be easier to overlook; especially because they deliver numerous movement benefits that you may not equate them with. For example, Conley emphasizes that power training isn’t just for athletes; it also has practical life applications. “Getting up and out of your chair, having good reaction time, and making sure you don’t fall if you step off a curb and trip are all part of that category,” she says.

Mobility means moving freely through a full range of motion, while balance helps you adjust to changing surfaces and react when your footing shifts—it isn’t just holding a tree pose. “There are thousands of nerve endings in each foot that help communicate to our brain where we are in space,” Perez explains. That feedback, combined with the feet’s ability to grip the ground, helps keep you steady.

Recovery is what allows your body to benefit from hard training, yet Conley says it’s often ignored: “I think one of the biggest mistakes is that people don’t recover.” Sleep, adequate nutrition, and lighter days that deliberately scale back workout volume or intensity give your body time to adapt and help you come back ready for your next workout.

The work you do in the gym should go beyond just trying to look good and prepare you for the demands of everyday movement. For strength and power work, Conley recommends deadlifts and kettlebell swings to train the hip-hinge pattern, along with farmer’s carries to build strength in the core and lower body. “I love all that functional movement,” she says. “A sled push is also great, because as your heel comes off the ground, you’re hitting all the intrinsic muscles of your foot.”

Certain machine exercises may not seem so functional but can address specific weaknesses. For instance, Conley says she often uses seated calf raises to strengthen the tissues around the Achilles and leg extensions to isolate the quadriceps. She also recommends plyometrics—quick, explosive jumping and hopping drills—to develop power. “Try double-leg and single-leg hops, forward and backward, side to side, and zigzag moves,” she says, recommending five or six sets of 10 reps per exercise for plyometric movements.

Ankle and big-toe mobility are number one on Conley’s priority list for things you should focus on outside of your regular workouts. “When you can’t propel through the ankle, you’re going to get there by extending the knee so you can push yourself forward,” she says. “People come in with knee or back pain when oftentimes it’s an ankle problem.” She suggests making mobility a regular part of the week rather than waiting until something feels stiff or restricted. Even a short dedicated session can help you maintain the range of motion your training requires.

Perez says your feet also adapt to the surface beneath you and absorb force. “If you think of your foot like a trampoline, every single step we take, whether walking or running, the foot needs to be able to lower, which is that mobility piece, then it needs to be able to spring back up.”

Perez recommends two simple drills to improve foot mobility and strength: the Foot Handshake, where you weave the fingers of one hand between the toes of the opposite foot and gently circle the foot at the ankle; and Lift, Spread, and Reach, where you lift all five toes, spread them apart, then reach them forward as you lower them.

Another way you can activate your feet during training is to choose your shoes wisely. When it comes to footwear, Perez has one non-negotiable regardless of the activity: a wide toe box that lets your toes spread naturally. “If your toes are more narrow than the ball of your foot, that tells me we’ve got some work to do,” she says. In practice, that can mean adding foot mobility and strength drills to your routine and choosing shoes that let your toes spread naturally.

Perez favors Altra Fit, both for her own footwear and when recommending shoes to others, because it gives the forefoot more room than a traditionally tapered toe box. Conley’s experience shows how the amount of cushioning that feels right can change over time as your foot gets stronger and needs more targeted footwear. She started out in the Altra FWD VIA 2, a cushioned shoe with the original (read: roomiest) FootShape™ and a 4 mm drop that felt familiar coming from conventional running shoes. “I was getting some toe splay and my foot was getting stronger,” she recalls. “Now I put them on, and it’s too much shoe for me because I don’t need as much cushioning.”

That’s where having options comes in. Altra’s Torin 9 offers a more moderate level of cushioning, standard footshape (secure midfoot), and a zero-drop platform that is good for running and still takes advantage of the Altra Fit that helps your feet get stronger as you log miles. For a lower-profile option, the Altra Escalante 5 has low cushioning, a 24 mm stack height, zero drop, and the original, roomiest FootShape fit.

“You’ll want to use the least amount of shoe assistance necessary for the activity,” Perez recommends. A lower-profile, more flexible shoe, like the Escalante 5, offers more ground feel for strength training, while extra cushioning or rocker geometry, found in the Torin 9 and FWD VIA 2, may be useful on longer runs. Conley agrees that a plush running shoe isn’t necessarily the best tool for lifting. “You can’t feel the ground,” she says of maximalist shoes. “You’re standing on something that decreases your sensory acuity.”

If multidimensional fitness is new to you, Conley recommends starting with manageable strength work (two or three days a week), walking, and one or two mobility or foot exercises, and build gradually as your strength and capacity improve. “Do things that challenge you, but not to the point where you start to feel overwhelmed,” she says.

If you already work out or run regularly, consider what’s missing from your routine while prioritizing your main goal. Conley suggests making room for mobility, balance, and power work, and fitting short foot-strength and mobility exercises into existing workouts. Do it while you’re fresh, adjusting your workload when running volume increases or recovery suffers.

The goal isn’t to do everything all the time or become an expert at every type of training. It’s to build a body that can keep doing the things you love. Run the trails. Lift the heavy stuff. Hike the mountain. Get down on the floor with your kids and grandkids—and have the strength and mobility to get back up again.

#4685. Zonveer ZX3 review: one of the best-value electric dirt bikes for beginners

The Zonveer ZX3 is one of the best values I’ve seen in electric off-road riding, and one of the most fun things I’ve ridden to date – value for the dollar. Its Black Friday sale brings the 2,800W electric dirt bike down to $1,299, $500 off its $1,799 list price.

For that money, you get a 1,200Wh battery, dual hydraulic disc brakes, and full suspension in a 130 lb package. That’s a great entry point for beginners.

Zonveer is a young brand. It launched in the US in March with two bikes, the kid-sized DX1 and the ZX3, and it’s run by United Mobility, which lists its address in Dover, Delaware. It sells direct and ships from US warehouses, and Zonveer also sells the ZX3 across Europe under its own brand through its EU store.

Here’s what the ZX3 brings, according to Zonveer’s product page:

A hub motor means there’s no motor chain to maintain, and the NFC card and PIN unlock mean there’s no app to fight with. I like that.

Zonveer sent me a ZX3 to test, and I’m impressed with what they shipped, knowing the cost. It isn’t trying to be a race bike. And it doesn’t need to be. Here’s my first ride review:

With 2,800W peak, it’s somewhat modest by e-moto standards. That’s exactly what makes it approachable for someone who has never ridden a dirt bike: the power is enough to have a blast on trails without being intimidating.

My girlfriend had never ridden a dirt bike before, and she got comfortable within a few minutes, and she was hooked as soon as she got the hang of it.

And while testing with my girlfriend, it was clear this bike makes the most sense for lighter riders. Zonveer claims it climbs slopes of up to 30 degrees, which is optimistic for anyone over ~175 lbs, like myself. It still climbed some of the worst slopes on my land, but it did so with some difficulty, which wasn’t the case for some of my lighter friends who also rode it.

Range is the other claim to take with a grain of salt. Riding 45 miles on 1,200Wh means using under 27Wh per mile, which is e-bike efficiency on a 130 lb dirt bike with knobby tires. It’s still a lot of energy, and you can ride this long distances at lower speeds. Just expect less if you ride it hard, and that’s where the fun is at.

Zonveer’s Black Friday sale has the ZX3 at $1,299, and the company gave Electrek readers the code ELECTREK for an extra 5% off, which brings it down to $1,234.05.

The sale also includes a free water bottle and lock, and can be combined for a two-pack of ZX3s for $2,599. Shipping is free, the warranty is one year, Zonveer told us it accepts returns within 30 days on bikes ridden less than 10 miles, with a $200 restocking fee. Here’s the full refund policy.

We’ve ridden a lot of electric two-wheelers, and the ZX3 is one of the most fun per dollar. At $1,299, or about $1,234 with our code, it’s hard to find another 1,200Wh electric dirt bike with dual hydraulic disc brakes and full suspension from a brand that ships from US warehouses.

It’s not fast by e-moto standards, and the range and climbing claims are optimistic. But for beginners, and especially lighter riders, the power lands right in that sweet spot of manageable fun. It’s a bike you can learn on without scaring yourself, and it’s cheap enough that a family can buy two for less than one Sur-Ron.

#4684. Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

They stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these new reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is important, especially for risk reduction.

She said issues with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg said.

Suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” said Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are important windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” said William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”

The authors note several age-related warning signs of heart issues. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” said Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

The authors of that report listed several steps they said could reverse these trends. Among them:

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu said.

Weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She said that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan said women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”

#4683. The 94 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 11 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4682. Tesla kills $41,990 Model Y AWD: all-wheel drive now costs $8,000 more

Tesla has pulled the $41,990 Model Y All-Wheel Drive from its US online configurator. The cheapest dual-motor Model Y you can order now is the Model Y Premium AWD at $49,990, an $8,000 jump.

The trim lasted just over nine months. Tesla launched it in early February, and it’s gone without a word from the company.

Here’s what Tesla’s US Model Y design studio lists as of today (prices before the destination fee):

When Tesla launched the base Model Y AWD in February, it was basically the stripped-down Model Y with a second motor. It had 294 miles of range, did 0-60 mph in 4.6 seconds and kept the same cut-down cabin as the base RWD. At a $2,000 premium over the single-motor version, it was the most sensible AWD pricing Tesla had offered in years.

And the AWD trim isn’t the only change. In February, the Premium RWD cost $44,990 and the Premium AWD cost $48,990. Both are now $1,000 higher.

Add it up and the cheapest all-wheel-drive Model Y went from $41,990 to $49,990 in nine months. That’s a 19% increase.

The timing isn’t great for Tesla’s competitive position. Chevrolet’s 2027 Equinox EV LT 1 AWD starts at $40,295 before destination, with 307 miles of EPA range. Ford’s Mustang Mach-E Select AWD starts at $40,795.

Both now undercut Tesla’s cheapest AWD crossover by more than $9,000.

If you live somewhere it snows and you were shopping for a new Model Y, the math just got a lot worse. You can still find some base AWD units in Tesla’s inventory, but once those are gone, that’s it.

This is also the latest cut in a year of Tesla shrinking its lineup. Elon Musk killed the Model S and Model X in January to free up Fremont for Optimus, and Cybertruck production is winding down. Meanwhile, the most recent new Tesla is the $61,990 Model Y L, which sits at the top of the range, not the bottom.

We liked this trim. It was the first time in a long time that Tesla treated all-wheel drive as a $2,000 option rather than a huge upsell bundled with a nicer interior, and it put the Model Y right in the price bracket of the Equinox EV and Mach-E with AWD.

Now it’s gone, and the Premium trims went up $1,000 on top of that. Tesla didn’t explain either move. It rarely does anymore.

There are two plausible reasons. Either Tesla is tight on Model Y build slots and would rather fill them with higher-margin Premium trims, or the cheap AWD simply wasn’t selling. We don’t know which. But both explanations land in the same place for buyers: a more expensive Model Y.

Tesla is not going to keep 6 different model Y trims especially when the most expensive trim in the Model YL is selling. They will definitely squeeze out as much money from selling more expensive trims so the lowest end trim will most likely be next to go.

And Tesla has a habit of this. The “Standard” name for its cheaper Model Y and Model 3 lasted a few months. The single-motor Cybertruck, the only version that made sense, was gone within days. Cheaper trims show up, get a news cycle, and quietly disappear.

That’s a problem for a company whose consumer lineup is shrinking down to two cars. The Model Y is Tesla’s volume. Thinning it out at the bottom is the opposite of what you’d do if growing EV sales were the priority.

How long before the $39,990 RWD goes the same way?

#4681. Behind the Kennel Doors of America's Animal Shelters

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

I’ve long been interested in the lives and fate of rescued dogs, the spirit of empathic kinship, the wonderful relationships that can developed between rescued dogs and their humans, why rescued dogs aren't any quirkier than other dogs, and why Psychology Today writer and dog expert stopped using the excuse, "Oh, she's a rescue dog." because her dog Bella didn't like to be touched by strangers and there is nothing wrong with this.

Writing about shelter and rescue dogs can be tricky business and I was very pleased to learn of a detailed and balanced view centering on the lives of these dogs who need all the care and love they can get. In her new highly acclaimed book Everydog: The Real Story of America's Shelter and Rescue Dogs ... and How You Can Help Them, the eclectic writer Eliza Rubenstein brings years of experience in different aspects of the world of dogs to the fore and offers "a compassionate, clear-eyed examination of the problem of homeless dogs in America."

Here's what Rubenstein had to say about these most complex issues while blending facts and research with interviews, stories, humor, and commentary.

Eliza Rubenstein: Every era of my life has been made better (okay, and a little messier) by dogs--living with them, training and showing them, writing about them, and working to find homes for the ones who need a place to go. A little over 30 years ago, my best friend and I wrote one of the earliest how-to books about dog adoption, and I've always thought that someday I'd write another book on the subject--not a how-to this time, but a deeper look into the fascinating world of sheltering and rescue for dog lovers who want to understand it better and become more effective allies.

ER: I wrote this book for everyone who loves and cares about dogs: those who have adopted (or been frustrated in their attempts to adopt) a dog, those who work in shelters or rescues, or those who simply find the subject interesting. It's conversational in tone and specifically designed to be more uplifting than it is depressing, since I know that's a concern for all of us with soft hearts!

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

ER: Everydog explores the nuance behind (and unpacks some of the confusion around) many of the hottest topics in sheltering. Why is it so hard to adopt when I keep hearing that there are too many dogs in shelters? What does "no-kill" really mean? Did people really return all their COVID adoptees to shelters after they went back to work? Can we really "save them all"?

There's a lot of incomplete and fragmented information on the internet about dog adoption, and a lot of it is wrapped up in emotion and anger, even to the point of misanthropy, so I'm interested in filling in the information gaps and helping to find some common ground among the various weary factions of people who care about them.

One of the constant themes in the book is that we can't help dogs if we alienate humans, because--as a very smart woman quoted in its pages says--"you need people to save animals."

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

ER: When I began to imagine what this book could be, I went searching for others on the subject; surely someone had already written a book for people who wanted to understand the world of dog sheltering, adoption, and homelessness. But nobody had.

There were (and are) great books on niche aspects of the field, and inspiring stories about particular dogs and people that offered important and insightful glimpses into it, yet I couldn't find anything quite like the one I was envisioning. And when you spend enough time in sheltering, you learn that there's no virtue in waiting around for someone else to do the work when you could be doing it yourself, so I started writing.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about the ins and outs and ups and downs of sheltering dogs they will come to appreciate what the dogs and humans go through to give the dogs the best lives possible?

ER: At least in my own life, I know that being the best possible ally and advocate means combining empathy with education. I hope Everydog will equip dog lovers with information they can use, while encouraging them to keep an open heart even on the days when that's difficult. But I also hope it will be a book they love reading! It's filled with stories of wonderful dogs, incredibly inspiring people, a lot of funny stuff, and plenty of my own "aha" moments and dog-driven learning curves.

There are sobering moments and difficult topics, but there are also so, so many reasons to be optimistic about the future of dogs in this country. It's my fondest hope that this book encourages readers to join that movement. Dogs are worth it.

In conversation with the eclectic Eliza Rubenstein, a writer and veteran of the animal-welfare world and co-author of The Adoption Option: Choosing and Raising the Shelter Dog For You.

#4680. Meta to deploy 25 electric semi trucks across I-10 corridor, but has nothing to ship

Electric truck operator Nevoya is expanding its deal with Meta with the fresh deployment of 25 Class 8 battery-electric trucks on the Interstate 10 (I-10) between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona … but Meta won’t be shipping any products.

The second major trucking deal between Facebook parent company Meta and electric truck operator Nevoya will put 25 new battery-electric semis on I-10, running freight between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona. But Meta isn’t buying trucks, hiring drivers or shipping its own products. Instead, Zuck’s company helping pay for someone else’s cleaner freight through environmental attribute certificates (EACs), a carbon credit mechanism that lets companies claim the emissions benefits of electric trucking without operating the trucks themselves.

“Coming back to Nevoya for a second corridor reflects what we look for in our value chain work: partners that can scale, and agreements we can repeat, said Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta. “Freight is part of the emissions footprint of building and operating our data centers, and multi-year commitments like this help address our scope 3 emissions and make electric trucking available and competitive on the routes that serve the regions where we build.”

Meta was one of several buyers in the DC-based Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) buyers’ alliance. The group’s collective EAC purchases supported Nevoya’s initial 63-truck deployment on the Houston–Dallas corridor back in May. This new Agreement, however, is a standalone deal between Nevoya and Meta only, and gives Meta an established framework to open more electric truck corridors in the future.

This clever application of these agreements is what makes the Dallas-Houston run stand out, with GMA calling it, “the first large-scale application of book and claim to zero-emission trucking.” The company adds that this arrangement helps client companies overcome existing barriers to EV adoption while enabling Nevoya to deploy new trucks, “where they deliver the strongest commercial and operational value.”

Yuck. That's the feeling I get when reading this. Am I happy that more EV semi's will be going on the road? Yes. But the way it's being done just makes me feel dirty. And I refuse to do or have anything that Mark Zuckerberg is involved with. I find him to be disgusting. But then again I find most of these super wealthy people to be vomit inducing.

So I'd liken this deal to a guy who goes out to a bar with the sole intention of "having some fun". And it doesn't matter to him how that happens, as long as he gets his happy ending. But then when the sun rises and the darkness vanishes, who this guy slept with is revealed and it's not good.

Zucherberg isn't doing any of this for the planet. He's doing it for money.

Nevoya expects Meta’s fresh batch of semis to begin prowling I-10 in 2027, where they’ll cover approximately 4 million freight miles annually.

#4678. Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to new research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, said Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she said.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

She said researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”

Weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he said. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

“It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy said.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy said. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

The study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham said adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive plan,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.
