#4567. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What a Missed Deadline Taught Me About Switching Off

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I missed a deadline last week. The piece you’re reading was supposed to be filed before I headed out on a long weekend to Italy for my wife’s birthday.

The main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece. An urgent stakeholder ask out of the blue, a couple of unanticipated work fire drills, and a long-standing evening social commitment earlier in the week made for a perfect storm, and something had to give.

The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.

It caught up with me at 6 am on the first morning, when I found myself drafting this column in my head. I should have been dozing peacefully. I continued to ruminate on my lengthy to-do list at work deep into day one as we headed from Venice into the Dolomites. My body was in Italy, but my brain was clearly still at my desk.

Switching off, particularly from work, is hard for most of us, and especially in an age of ubiquitous screens and wall-to-wall information competing for our attention. For me, that always-on reality plays a major role in the difficulties I have disconnecting from the daily grind.

I’m fortunate to love my job, and if I’m candid, I probably take a little too much of my identity from it. I hold on tight, and the phone in my pocket is an ever-present enabler.

A meme that has stuck with me over the years goes something along the lines of being an adult is staring at medium screens all day only to come home and stare at a little screen while a big screen is on in the background. The irony is not lost on me that I came across this rather withering take on modern life while scrolling on said little screen.

Regardless of the role the screen plays, psychologists who study employee well-being describe what I was missing for the early part of the weekend as “psychological detachment.” A state where you are genuinely able to not think about work while away from it. The science suggests it’s an important thing to work on.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 32 studies found that vacationing has a strong effect on well-being, and that the effect lasts longer than earlier research suggested. A second, smaller analysis of eight studies points to detaching from work, along with physical activity, as among the most helpful things to do while you’re off. In another study that tracked teachers during a two-week break, exhaustion, anxiety, and low mood all declined, while those who kept ruminating about work recovered less.

Whatever the science says, I know that for me the act of stepping away from work and being disciplined about not checking back in while I’m away is critical for my mental health and for staving off burnout. Getting out in nature and hiking or cycling or swimming keeps me present. It resets and recharges my batteries, and it tops up my creativity in a way that I find benefits what I am then able to bring back to the office.

Sure enough, as we drove deeper into the mountains on a crisp, blue-sky day, I could feel the golden autumnal hues and majestic rock formations drawing me in, closer to an elemental feeling of calm and happiness. That sense of equilibrium stayed with me all weekend, and while I’d be lying if I said my mind didn’t occasionally drift to my desk, it was fleeting, with the knowledge that all the things would be waiting for me when I got back. Just like this piece was.

With Thanksgiving on the horizon, and the holidays coming thick and fast thereafter, I’ll leave you with this bit of hard-earned advice: if your job is deeply entwined with your life and part of who you are, as mine is, time away can sometimes feel like a small act of disloyalty. It isn’t. In fact, it’s probably the most important thing you can do to remain faithful to your work ethic, and to yourself.

And if you’ll be working over the holidays, or you’re not working right now, or you don’t have the benefit of someone on hand to carry some of the load for you (shout out to all the Grannies out there), or your vacation looks very different from mine, that’s all okay. Find the pockets where and when you can: an evening, a walk, an hour in front of a screen, or better yet a book, and let work wait. Above all else, be kind to yourself. That’s how you really give yourself a break.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4565. Think Someone Envies You? Here’s Why You Might Be Wrong

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

As the holidays approach, you're likely to meet new people and socialize with colleagues and family you don't normally see the rest of the year.

In such settings, you're also more likely to come into situations where you sense a bit of "healthy competition." Turkey Trot, anyone? You may also interact with people playing the "one-up" game, where someone shares a more intense version of the story or situation you just shared.

Whenever people gather, we're assessing and comparing. Everyone does it. It's natural. It helps us understand how we fit in and get cues on how to behave.

Envy not only can occur, but it can also help you navigate these times...though not in the way most people expect.

When some people discover I've written a book on envy, but they are not yet aware of its contents, they will tell me, "I don't feel envy, but I know a lot of people who do." They will then proceed to tell me about the people who envy them.

They don't know that I believe that everyone envies. It is a universal emotion. Unpleasant, yes, but not necessarily a harmful one.

I get it. In this culture where envy is often seen as a deadly sin, it's hard to admit feeling envy.

But not acknowledging one's own envy is unfortunate because you miss out on all that envy can reveal to you. However, that isn't the mistake I want to focus on here. I believe the bigger mistake is to assume that you know when someone else is feeling envy.

First, we can't be certain it is envy they are feeling. Not only is it impossible to read minds, but we also can't reliably detect envy from their faces. As envy researcher Jens Lange told me, "If there were [a unique envy facial expression], we would likely suppress it."

Second, when we ascribe envy to someone else, we create an artificial barrier. We make a negative judgment about their character and lower their status to elevate ourselves. Not even conscious of this, we begin to operate on the false assumption and the distance we've created. It subtly impacts our interactions and our behaviors.

First, adopt a curious mindset. It's harder to stop your mind from thinking of something than it is to suggest something new to consider. So, instead of saying, "Don't judge or make assumptions," try, "I don't know their story." Remind yourself that you don't know what happened in their past, what just happened moments ago, what their circumstances are, or what their mood is.

Second, dial up the warmth. Amy Cuddy, Susan Fiske, and Peter Glick's research revealed that when people encounter one another, they ask two questions: "Does this person want to harm or help me?" and "Is this person capable of following through with their threat or assistance?" They found that people tend to be envied when they are not warm but competent. So, if it is true that you're envied, more reason to approach with warmth.

During your year-end holiday festivities, try combining these two concepts and adopt a "warm curiosity."

You may walk away learning unexpected reasons why you like someone you didn't before.

Alicke, M. D., & Zell, E. (2008). Social Comparison and Envy. In R. Smith (Ed.), Envy: Theory and Research (pp. 73–93). Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195327953.003.0005

Cuddy, A. J. C., Glick, P., & Beninger, A. (2011). The dynamics of warmth and competence judgments, and their outcomes in organizations. Research in Organizational Behavior, 31, 73–98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.riob.2011.10.004

Lange, J. (2025). [In discussion with the author].

#4564. Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember.

Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.

Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.

The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.

Solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.

That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.

In the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.

The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.

“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember.

By combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.

The researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.

That’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.

Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.

The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants.

Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.

In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.

Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.

For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.

Good way to think about the whole system. So what exactly does Don not-Quixote have against windmills?

Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets users explore reliable electricity costs in their own region.

#4561. Hailey Bieber Says She's Been Diagnosed With PMDD: What Are the Signs, Symptoms?

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Hailey Bieber is sharing her experience with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a condition she says has fueled her growing interest in women’s health research.

The Rhode Beauty founder recently announced a $5 million, three-year partnership with the Foundation for Women’s Health in an interview with Women’s Wear Daily (WWD).

“As a woman, I feel frustrated by the lack of research, the lack of awareness, the lack of certain conversation around it,” Bieber told WWD.

Motherhood has also shaped her perspective. Bieber welcomed her son, Jack Blues, with her husband, Justin Bieber, in 2024, describing the experience as a “really intense and special journey.”

She also shared that she “struggled” with PMDD after giving birth, noting that there’s “not a lot of conversation or research around it.”

“When we can identify with each other and have conversations relating to each other and talking about the things we’re dealing with and struggling with, I do think it makes it feel like less of a lonely journey,” Bieber said.

PMDD is a complexcondition that causes severe physical and psychological symptoms that typically occur in the days or weeks leading up to menstruation.

“What distinguishes PMDD from the more common PMS (premenstrual syndrome) is the severity of the symptoms and how significantly they can interfere with daily functioning,” Sari Eitches, MD, dual board certified physician and medical advisor to Terra Mare, told Healthline.

“Another defining feature is the timing: symptoms typically worsen in the week or two before a period, resolve within a few days after menstruation begins, and are minimal or absent during the rest of the cycle,” she said.

Eitches also noted that PMDD is a chronic condition that can affect women at any stage of their reproductive lives, from adolescence through perimenopause, as long as they are having menstrual cycles.

“It is caused by a sensitivity to cyclic hormonal and neurotransmitter fluctuations, so [it] can occur in anyone with a menstrual cycle, though stages of hormonal fluctuation- including postpartum, weaning breastfeeding, and perimenopause- can be a trigger,” she added.

According to research published in 2024, approximately 1.6% of women and girls meet the strict diagnostic criteria for PMDD, equivalent to an estimated 31 million people worldwide.

A higher percentage of 3.2% have a provisional diagnosis, meaning a healthcare professional may believe a person has PMDD, but symptoms have not been measured for a sustained amount of time to meet the criteria for a confirmed diagnosis.

Eitches said that women with a personal or family history of depression or anxiety may be more prone to developing PMDD, as are women with a family history of PMDD itself.

“PMDD is understood to be caused by a combination of heritable biological sensitivities and environmental triggers. These can include a history of trauma, chronic stress, and other chronic medical conditions,” she noted.

Eitches also said that you should consider seeing a doctor if your symptoms are severe enough that they’re interfering with your ability to go to work or school, maintain your relationships, or participate in your life in the same way that you do during the other weeks of the month.

To diagnose PMDD, a healthcare professional will review your medical history and symptoms and may perform a physical exam. They will typically ask you to track your symptoms over at least two menstrual cycles.

A PMDD diagnosis generally requires at least five symptoms, including at least one mood-related symptom, that occur before menstruation, improve shortly after a period begins, and significantly interfere with daily life.

Treatment options for PMDD include prescription medications and over-the-counter treatments that may help relieve certain symptoms, such as:

Eitches noted that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can also help manage symptoms.

Lifestyle changes may also help manage PMDD symptoms, including practicing relaxation techniques, eating a balanced diet, limiting sugary and salty foods, and getting regular physical activity.

Eitches noted that getting enough high quality sleep and resting on a consistent schedule is also important.

“I also recommend focusing on a whole-foods-based diet, limiting added sugar and caffeine, and avoiding cigarette smoking,” she said.

#4559. Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.

The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.

When Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.

That plan didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.

The bigger issue is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.

No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.

For a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.

But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.

As we reported last week, Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”

It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.

The Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also says only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.

The subscription agreement carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.

So you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.

The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.

Tesla first showed what looked like a wireless home charging station during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.

Tesla then filed patents for the charging pad and, after the Cybercab unveiling, released a video of it charging the robotaxi at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.

And that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.

With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.

Tesla’s own plans for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.

Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.

The other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also announced a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.

Neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t announced one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.

This is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.

Musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also said “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.

That saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.

I don't see any evidence that the production Cybercab has the onboard hardware to use such a pad. Besides the wireless receiver coil it would need some kind of charging hardware to convert the pulsed wireless charging into DC to charge the battery.

If you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.

The fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.

Will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it launches, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is currently basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.

If you’re buying an EV, how you charge it at home matters as much as the car itself, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. The ID. Polo GTI “brings the legendary GTI driving pleasure into the electric future,” VW said after opening pre-orders last month.

Volkswagen previewed a mysterious new hot hatch draped under a cloth that appears to be a souped-up version of the ID. Polo GTI. Despite its attempt to “hide” it, you can see the massive rear wing and wide wheel arches under the cloth.

The company promised that “something really spicy” will be served this Friday, November 20, with the tags #Volkswagen, #GTI, and #GTI50.

Although no other details were revealed, the new hot hatch is thought to be the more powerful “Clubsport” variant.

A post shared by Volkswagen (@volkswagen)

Volkswagen’s head of driving dynamics, Florian Umbach, told Autocar earlier this year that the company is planning to launch the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport, a more powerful variant that will deliver close to 300 hp, up from 223 hp in the standard model.

Umbach said that Volkswagen is developing “a similar kind of paddleshift power delivery that the Hyundai N cars have” for the upcoming electric hot hatch.

Hyundai’s performance EVs, the IONIQ 5 N and IONIQ 6 N, feature a simulated gear-shifting system called N e-Shift that uses paddle shifters on the steering wheel to replicate the feel of an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission. It works with the N Active Sound+ system to make it feel like you’re in a traditional gas-powered sports car.

It has yet to be confirmed whether the hot hatch debuting on Friday is, in fact, the new ID. Polo Clubsport, but the design clues give us a good idea of what’s coming.

Man, $45k for a starting price is a little uncomfortably steep for a hatch, given there are a little bigger options in that range. I wish it started somewhere in the 30s to be competitive.

Check back on Friday for the full details.

Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000).

Like the first Golf GTI from 1976, the electric ID. Polo GTI uses a front-wheel-drive powertrain. The front-mounted electric motor delivers 223 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft (290 Nm) of instant torque, enabling it to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.8 seconds.

In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the ID.3 GTI, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.

#4556. Does Menopausal Hormone Therapy Lower Dementia Risk? Timing and Genetics May Hold the Answer

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a new study.

The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.

The findings could offer new insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.

Researchers also found that certain associations between hormone therapy and brain health differed depending on whether women carried a genetic variant associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

However, the relationship between estrogen and brain health is complex. While the findings suggest that longer estrogen exposure may be associated with healthier brain aging, they do not establish that hormone therapy can prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

The researchers drew data from the Gothenburg H70-1944 Birth Cohort, a longitudinal study of 1,203 individuals born in 1944 who resided in Gothenburg, Sweden.

The final cohort included 352 cisgender women, with an average age of 70, who had no neurological disorders and reliable self-reported data on their estrogen exposure.

Individual estrogen exposure was measured through structured interviews. It included:

The researchers used this information as a proxy for lifetime estrogen exposure, though the study didn’t measure actual hormone levels.

Participants were also given a brain MRI at baseline and then again at a 5-year follow-up.

The researchers found that those with a longer reproductive span had a lower risk of small vessel disease (SVD). Participants with a longer reproductive life span had an 8% lower risk of having two or more signs of SVD. However, later menopause, rather than earlier menstruation, appeared to be the main driver of this association.

Those who used MHT also tended to have fewer signs of SVD and better microstructural integrity in the white matter.

In individuals who carried the APOE-ε4 variant, which increases a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s disease, MHT was associated with greater cortical thickness in brain regions vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease. However, there was no association for those without this variant.

The researchers noted that longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and white matter trajectories over time.

Dung Trinh, MD, internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that estrogen has several important effects on the brain that may help support cognitive health.

It influences communication between brain cells, supports the brain’s ability to use glucose for energy, helps regulate neurotransmitters, and plays a role in maintaining healthy blood vessels and reducing inflammation and oxidative stress.

“As estrogen levels decline during menopause, some of these protective effects may diminish. Replacing estrogen closer to the menopause transition could potentially help preserve some of these functions during a vulnerable period for brain health,” he said. “While these findings are encouraging, MHT has not been proven to prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.”

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed and noted, “Starting menopausal hormone therapy earlier in the menopause transition may help minimize some changes by supporting the brain during this period of hormonal fluctuation.”

“There is growing interest in whether early estrogen therapy may also help reduce the long-term risk of Alzheimer’s disease, although more research is needed before we can establish that benefit,” she added.

Ross told Healthline that this research reinforces the importance of recognizing menopause as more than a reproductive or hormonal transition.

“We know that women are disproportionately affected by dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, and some women experience noticeable cognitive changes beginning in perimenopause,” she said. “If future research confirms that starting hormone therapy earlier can help protect long-term cognitive health, it could influence how we approach menopause treatment and encourage more proactive conversations between women and their healthcare providers.”

“The goal should be to individualize treatment based on a woman’s symptoms, medical history, and overall health rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach,” Ross added.

Trinh agreed that an individualized approach to menopause management is important.

“This does not mean that every woman should start hormone therapy to prevent dementia. Instead, it highlights the importance of understanding which women might benefit, when treatment should begin, and which formulations are most appropriate,” he said. “Factors such as age, time since menopause, cardiovascular risk, metabolic health, family history, and potentially genetic factors may all help guide future recommendations.”

“We still need stronger clinical evidence before changing current prescribing guidelines specifically for dementia prevention,” Trinh added.
